transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19
Start time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Laura Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SRE); Priya Rao (Nova ML Eng), Michael Chen (Nova Infra Lead), Elena Torres (Director of ML), Josh Park (MLOps)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on quantization tradeoffs for Nova's gen-2 LLM workloads. Covered INT8 vs FP8, GPTQ vs AWQ toolchains, observed accuracy regressions on safety/precision prompts, and production rollout strategies (VPC/on-prem, Dedicated pool). Agreed next steps to run a short pilot and share benchmark artifacts.

Topics: quantization (INT8/FP8), GPTQ/AWQ, accuracy regression tracking, KV cache behavior with quantized kernels, batching effects on tail latency, VPC/Dedicated pilot, rollback to float16.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Laura (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a ~45-60 minute technical review, Samir's gonna drive the quant bits and then we'll go into infra questions. Quick intro?
[00:12] Priya (Nova): Hi, Priya here — ML eng on Nova's gen-2 projects. We're looking to cut inference cost while keeping response accuracy for our summarization and safety checks.
[00:20] Michael (Nova): Michael — infra. We'll be running tests in our VPC, possibly a Dedicated pool at Redwood.
[00:26] Samir (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. I'll start with a quick primer on the toolchains we typically use — GPTQ and AWQ — and then show numbers. Note, transcription may swap a few acronyms, sorry in advance.
[00:38] Samir: So, at a high level: GPTQ gives you a post-training quantization path that is layerwise and generally stable for many models; AWQ is newer and often yields better accuracy at 4-bit and offers int8-ish performance with lower memory. But implementation differences matter — kernel selection, per-channel vs per-tensor scaling, and how attention KV caches are stored.
[00:55] Elena (Nova): Quick Q: when you say "KV cache stored", do you mean it's kept in fp16 even when the model is int8?
[00:59] Samir: Good question. In many setups we keep KV cache as FP16 to avoid attention head degradation, but there are AWQ/GPQ flags that try compressed KV formats. In practice for low-latency streaming we prefer KV in fp16 — reduces accuracy regressions for long context.
[01:15] Priya: We're seeing weird hallucination upticks when we tried bitsandbytes 8-bit on our safety prompts. Curious if that's expected.
[01:20] Samir: Yup, bitsandbytes int8 can introduce distribution shifts for certain tokens. Two things happen — outlier detection and range folding — leading to subtle logits shifts. GPTQ tends to be more conservative; AWQ often wins on subjective accuracy but requires careful calibration on the quant scales.
[01:35] Diego (Redwood SRE): Also kernel selection: the runtime will pick different GEMM kernels based on quant format and sequence length — you might see throughput regressions for very short sequences because the overhead of dequantize/reorder isn't amortized.
[01:50] Michael: That matches us — most of our calls are 30-80 tokens. Latency is super important.
[01:55] Samir: Right, so two knobs: prefer INT8 with per-channel scales and keep KV as fp16; or go minimal-accuracy AWQ with selective fp16 layers (first/last) to reduce regressions. We measured for a 7B family model: FP16 baseline p50 latency 110ms, INT8 (GPTQ optimized) p50 82ms with ~0.7% accuracy delta on our BLEU-like metric, AWQ 78ms with ~0.4% delta but slightly worse tail p95.
[02:22] Priya: Can you show the raw diffs?
[02:24] Samir: I'll share the sheet afterwards — but here's a paraphrase of the numbers I have: baseline FP16 perplexity X, INT8 GPTQ +1.8% on perplexity, AWQ +0.9%, FP8 experiments are mixed — hardware support inconsistent, and FP8 often requires recompiled kernels.
[02:45] Josh (Nova): We don't have FP8 in our fleet yet — too bleeding edge. Any fallback strategy suggestions?
[02:50] Samir: Always include a float16 fallback route and a canary rollout. Redwood's rollout can do per-route model variant selection with automatic fallback to a float16 variant if quality drifts beyond thresholds. We also support a per-prompt eval hook so you can monitor specific prompt families and trigger rollbacks.
[03:07] Elena: Can you elaborate on the eval hooks? How do we define thresholds?
[03:11] Samir: You can register a small eval set; we compute BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim deltas and you configure thresholds — e.g., <1% embedding sim drop or <0.5% safety regression. If exceeded, automatic traffic shifts happen.
[03:24] Priya: Our biggest worry: safety edge cases. Even small numeric shifts can flip a safety classifier. Any known mitigation?
[03:29] Samir: Two mitigations: 1) keep toxic-detection models in higher precision (float16) or run them as separate model calls; 2) apply per-layer selective quantization — leave head or layernorm layers in float16. GPTQ supports selective reconstruction for critical layers.
[03:45] Michael: What's overhead for selective fp16 layers? Memory-wise and perf-wise?
[03:48] Samir: Minor memory increase — maybe 5-12% depending on layers picked. Perf-wise, it's usually fine we saw p50 change by 2-6ms but can significantly reduce accuracy regressions.
[03:58] Laura (Redwood AE): Quick interjection — on the Dedicated side we can reserve nodes with lower quantization overhead and test kernels tuned to AWQ; that's what we propose for the pilot.
[04:07] Michael: For VPC peering, will we need any special egress or firewall changes?
[04:11] Diego: You need standard VPC peering and allowed egress for metrics and log shipping; if you're using on-prem we'll offer a private data plane. We'll send a checklist.
[04:19] Priya: On batching — we noticed batching improves throughput but increases p95 latency. Any recommendations for mixed workloads?
[04:25] Samir: Use dynamic batching with latency-based cutoffs and sequence-length aware scheduling. Redwood supports continuous batching with max wait time caps; for high-priority interactive routes you set smaller max wait and higher cost per-token. Also warm KV caching reduces per-request token compute.
[04:40] Priya: How does quantization affect KV cache size?
[04:44] Samir: If you quantize weights but keep KV fp16, the cache size is unchanged. There are compressed-KV approaches in AWQ where KV is 8-bit packed; that reduces memory but increases decode overhead and can hurt long-context accuracy.
[04:58] Elena: Any rule of thumb for when to compress KV?
[05:01] Samir: If your context > 16k and memory is the bottleneck, try compressed KV with heavy eval; for <8k context keep KV fp16.
[05:10] Priya: We also run rerankers and embeddings — do you recommend quantizing those too?
[05:14] Samir: Embeddings models are sensitive — usually keep them at fp16 or use dedicated lower-bit models that were trained for quantization. Rerankers depend on similarity thresholds; small shifts are tolerable but run regression suites.
[05:25] Josh: Any support for automated per-route cost estimation when we flip to quantized models?
[05:29] Laura: Yes, Redwood Console shows token-level cost breakdowns, expected per-token cost for quantized vs fp16, and you can simulate monthly run rate. We'll include a sample cost sheet.
[05:39] Michael: Back to accuracy regressions — you mentioned +0.7% accuracy delta earlier. How do you define that across different tasks?
[05:45] Samir: It's task-dependent; for summarization we use ROUGE-L delta; for code generation we use exact-match on test suites, for safety we use classifier flip rate. We always report multiple metrics.
[05:55] Priya: Can you share the exact command flags you use for GPTQ and AWQ? The small differences in calibration make a big difference.
[06:01] Samir: Absolutely — we'll share the runbook. Example: GPTQ with per-channel scales, warmup=32 samples, blocksize=128, and AWQ with group size 128, quant type 'mse' vs 'amax' — there are nuances. We'll include recommended defaults and a note about re-run seeding because some libraries have nondeterministic heuristics.
[06:20] Elena: Are there any licensing or IP issues with these toolchains?
[06:24] Laura: Most of the libraries are open-source but check model licensing; Redwood's platform is agnostic. We'll include a short legal note in the packet.
[06:32] Priya: For the pilot, we'd like to see: 1) accuracy matrix across 50 safety & 50 domain prompts, 2) latency p50/p95 for 30/80 token ranges, 3) cost delta. Can Redwood produce that?
[06:41] Samir: Yes, if you provide the eval set we can run parallel tests on Dedicated nodes and give you the sheet. We'll also log per-prompt diffs to help triage regressions.
[06:49] Michael: Regarding rolling back, how immediate is the float16 fallback?
[06:52] Samir: You can set automatic rollback to trigger in seconds; it will shift traffic to the float16 variant and notify via webhook.
[06:57] Josh: Any gotchas for sequence length trimming and padding with quantized kernels?
[07:01] Samir: Padding overhead becomes more visible with quantized kernels because dequantize ops are per-tile; prefer token packing strategies and pad to nearest compute-friendly block to reduce wasted cycles. We'll share best-practices.
[07:12] Priya: One more on FP8 — you mentioned it's inconsistent. Are there accelerators that do FP8 well?
[07:17] Samir: Some newer GPUs and vendor runtimes support FP8 but it's not yet standard in our public Dedicated offerings. FP8 gives best density but often needs model-retraining or special conversion. For now we advise INT8/AWQ as practical middle ground.
[07:30] Elena: Sounds reasonable. Anything else on security/VPC?
[07:33] Diego: For Dedicated/VPC we support customer-managed KMS, audit logs, and SAML SSO. For on-prem we can ship the runtime with telemetry opt-in. We'll share the checklist.
[07:43] Laura: Ok, let's recap next steps — Samir to share quantization artifacts and runbook, Priya to run internal evals, Michael to confirm pilot window, Laura to send pricing and runbook.
[07:53] Priya: Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[07:55] Laura: Thanks — we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule the pilot.

End of meeting.
